meta.title: Award eligible-field sizes, campaign costs, and documented effects of nominations and wins
meta.companionTo: docs/research/world/research-career-depth.json (awards section: bodies, categories, calendars, nominee counts)
meta.method: WebSearch and WebFetch. PDFs that the fetch tool could not read (Television Academy fee schedule, Sylvestre et al. 2006, Rossman and Schilke 2014, NATAS Daytime call for entries) were text-extracted locally from the downloaded file and read directly.
meta.rules: No invented numbers. Where a figure was not found, value is null with a note. 'confirmed' is true when the figure was read from the primary source or from a named trade report of it; false when it came only from a search-engine summary, a secondary aggregator, or a count made by the fetch tool.
corrections: The brief cites 'Redelmeier & Singh 1999'. The paper is Redelmeier DA, Singh SM. Survival in Academy Award-winning actors and actresses. Annals of Internal Medicine 2001;134(10):955-962. Sylvestre et al. 2006 opens with 'In an article published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2001, Redelmeier and Singh reported...'.
The brief's example of 323 eligible films is the 97th Academy Awards (2025 ceremony). The 98th (2026 ceremony) list was 317.

The Reminder List carries up to 10 actresses and 10 actors per film (see research-career-depth.json), so the performer pool is bounded by films x 20 but the Academy does not publish a performer count.

daytimeEmmys.note: Not found. NATAS does not publish per-category submission counts for the Daytime acting categories. Its rule, which shapes the pool: in categories with 4 to 10 submissions the default number of nominations is 50% of submissions, rounded up (53rd Daytime Emmys call for entries). whatACampaignIs.description: A 'For Your Consideration' campaign is paid by the distributor or studio: trade and outdoor advertising, screenings and Q&As, events, publicists, and screeners. Screeners to Academy members may only be delivered digitally via the Academy Screening Room or a private link through an Academy-approved mailing house; digital screeners must be closed-captioned and may not carry extra material such as interviews or behind-the-scenes footage.

boxOffice.study: Deuchert E, Adjamah K, Pauly F. For Oscar Glory Or Oscar Money? Journal of Cultural Economics 2005;29:159-176.
findings: A Best Picture or Best Actor nomination raises weekly box office in the following weeks by more than 200%.
A Best Actress nomination raises it by about 150%.
The effect comes mainly from the nomination; winning adds little, except Best Actress, where winning produces substantially larger revenue than a nomination alone.
The prospect of a nomination gives studios an incentive to release late in the year.

boxOffice.study: Nelson RA, Donihue MR, Waldman DM, Wheaton C. What's an Oscar Worth? Economic Inquiry 2001;39(1):1-16.
findings: A nomination in a major category can add up to $4.8 million to a film's box office; a win up to $12 million.
boxOffice.confirmedNote: figures from search summary; paper not read

boxOffice.study: Rossman G, Schilke O. Close, But No Cigar: The Bimodal Rewards to Prize-Seeking. American Sociological Review 2014;79(1):86-108.
findings: Oscar nominations have a strong positive relationship with financial returns.

Net of nominations, 'Oscar appeal' (films built to court the Academy) has an appreciable negative effect on returns: prize-seeking pays above normal for those who get nominated and below normal for those who don't.
Without the nomination term, the effect of Oscar appeal is near zero (t = .75), consistent with rent dissipation: the expected value of prize-seeking is zero.
Illustration: Brokeback Mountain and The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada (both ~$15 million budgets, Dec 2005): eight nominations and $83 million domestic versus none and $9 million.

actorPayAndCasting.study: Sweeney K. Economics senior honors thesis, Colgate University, 2010 (reported by Colgate 2014 and Forbes 2013/2016).
findings: Winning Best Actor increases a male winner's salary by 81%, holding other variables constant.
Average post-win salary increase close to $3.9 million for men and under $0.5 million for women.
For women the win had no statistically significant effect on salary in some specifications; actresses' salaries seemed to decrease.
Average age at winning about 43.1 for men and 31.1 for women in the sample.
actorPayAndCasting.caveat: Undergraduate thesis, not peer-reviewed; dataset built from IMDb and Box Office Mojo.
actorPayAndCasting.confirmedNote: Both pages returned 403 or were unreadable; figures from search summaries quoting them.

actorPayAndCasting.claim: Agents report an Oscar win typically raises the asking price for the next film by about 20%; other reporting cites 20-60%.

actorPayAndCasting.study: Rossman G, Esparza N, Bonacich P. I'd Like to Thank the Academy, Team Spillovers, and Network Centrality. American Sociological Review 2010;75(1):31-51.
findings: Top-10 credited roles in films released 1936-2005.

An actor's chance of an Oscar nomination rises with the quality of collaborators (director, writer, co-stars): talent spills over onto the team, and high-skilled workers attach to one another, a mechanism of cumulative advantage.

actorPayAndCasting.study: Rotman School of Management (University of Toronto) and Carnegie Mellon University, 2011 ('Oscar curse').
findings: 751 Best Actor and Best Actress nominees, 1936-2010.
Best Actress winners were 63% more likely to divorce than nominees who did not win.
Average marriage after the award: 4.3 years for winners, 9.5 years for non-winners.
No such effect for Best Actor winners.

lifespan.study: Redelmeier DA, Singh SM. Survival in Academy Award-winning actors and actresses. Annals of Internal Medicine 2001;134(10):955-962.
findings: Life expectancy 3.9 years longer for Oscar winners than less recognised performers (controls).
28% reduction in death rates for winners (P = 0.003).
lifespan.flaw: Winners were classified as winners from birth, crediting the years before the win ('immortal time') to the award.
lifespan.confirmedNote: Numbers verified as quoted in Sylvestre et al. 2006.

lifespan.study: Sylvestre MP, Huszti E, Hanley JA. Do Oscar Winners Live Longer than Less Successful Peers? A Reanalysis of the Evidence. Annals of Internal Medicine 2006;145(5):361-363.
findings: On updated data, the original method gave 3.7 years and a 26% reduction (P = 0.006).

Correcting for immortal time and adjusting for sex and year of birth, winners against controls: 15% mortality reduction (CI -5% to 32%, P = 0.129 time-dependent Cox; CI -6% to 32%, P = 0.161 performer-years), an average advantage of 0.7 year (CI -0.3 to 1.6).
Winners against nominees: 18% reduction (CI -4% to 35%), an average advantage of 1.0 year (CI -0.2 to 2.0), not significant.
Ignoring immortal time produces an artificial longevity advantage of 0.8 year (winners against nominees) and 1.7 years (winners against controls).
20.7% of actresses won the year of their first nomination.
lifespan.conclusion: Once corrected, the data do not show that winning an Oscar lengthens life.

lifespan.study: Han X et al. (authors beyond first not verified). The effect of winning an Oscar Award on survival: correcting for healthy performer survivor bias with a rank preserving structural accelerated failure time model. Annals of Applied Statistics 2011;5(2A).
findings: Further correction for healthy-performer survivor bias. Effect sizes not retrieved.

lifespan.study: Redelmeier DA, Singh SM (as reported on the PLOS page). Long-term mortality of academy award winning actors and actresses. PLOS ONE 2022;17(4):e0266563.
findings: Winners against controls: 5.1-year absolute increase in life expectancy (95% CI 3.0-7.2).
41% improvement in mortality hazard (95% CI 19%-68%, p < 0.001).
Mean age at death 77.1 (winners) against 73.6 (controls).
Advantage tied to winning, not to nomination alone; larger in recent eras, for those who won younger, and for multiple winners.
lifespan.caveat: Authors' own follow-up; whether it fully answers the immortal-time critique was not assessed here.

television.study: Luminate, 'The Emmy Effect' (2024 Emmys, streaming minutes viewed, week 37 to week 38/39)
findings: Hacks (Outstanding Comedy Series): 5.4 million to 13.3 million minutes (+146%), then 19.7 million (+48%).
Baby Reindeer (Outstanding Limited or Anthology Series): 8.4 million to 48.8 million minutes (+481%), then +99%.
Shogun (Outstanding Drama Series): +345% week 37 to 38, then -12%.
The Bear season 2 (no win): +71% week 37 to 38 (spillover).

television.study: Parrot Analytics, effect of Emmy wins on demand for digital originals
findings: Seven Seconds: demand up 560% the day after the Emmys (more than 11.5 million Demand Expressions).

television.claim: Industry reporting: an Emmy win is not a direct financial windfall by ad sales, renewal price or syndication value, but has helped rescue low-rated, acclaimed young shows (Cheers, All in the Family cited).

television.note: No peer-reviewed study of an Emmy nomination's or win's effect on an individual actor's subsequent pay was found.
